client: I got some news from my doctor a few weeks ago that I'm still trying to process — I was diagnosed with a chronic illness, and honestly, it's been really hard to wrap my head around. Every day I wake up and there's this immediate wave of fear, like my whole future just got rewritten without my permission. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the diagnosis isn't going away no matter what I say in here.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — receiving news that reshapes how you see your future, and then waking up each morning to that wave of fear, takes a real toll. You're right that talking won't change the diagnosis itself, and I want to honor that reality rather than gloss over it; what we *can* work on together is how you relate to that fear and the story your mind is telling you about what this means for your life. What does that "rewritten future" look like when that wave of fear hits you in the morning — what thoughts tend to come with it?

client: When that wave hits in the morning, it's mostly this image of me becoming completely dependent on other people, like losing the ability to do the things that make me feel like myself. And then right behind that comes this thought that I'm going to end up alone through all of it, because who wants to stick around and watch someone deteriorate. It's not even a fully formed thought, it's more like this cold dread that just sits in my chest before I've even fully woken up.
therapist: That cold dread settling in before you're even fully awake — before you've had a chance to think or defend against it — sounds exhausting and deeply painful, like your nervous system is bracing for a loss that hasn't fully happened yet. I'm struck by those two fears together: losing yourself *and* being left alone in it, because they both point to something really important about what you value — your independence and your connections. I'd gently want to explore that second thought with you — when you imagine the people in your life, is there evidence that tells you they're the kind of people who leave, or is that the fear doing the talking?

client: That question kind of stops me, because honestly... most of the people in my life haven't actually left. But I think what scares me is that I've never really needed them before, not like this, and I don't know if they'll stick around when I'm not the version of myself they're used to. It feels less like evidence of who they are and more like I'm terrified of finding out.
therapist: There's something really honest and courageous in what you just said — you're not catastrophizing without awareness, you're sitting with a genuine uncertainty, and that's different. What I notice is that the fear isn't really "they will leave" — it's "I don't know if I can bear needing them and finding out," which makes sense when your independence has been such a core part of how you've held yourself together. I'm wondering — what does needing people mean to you, deep down? Is there a belief underneath this about what it says about you if you do need them?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think deep down I believe that needing people means I'm a burden, or that I'm weak, like I haven't figured out how to be enough on my own. And there's this voice that says if I let myself need someone and they pull away, that's proof I was right to keep people at a distance all along.
therapist: That belief — that needing others makes you a burden or proves some kind of insufficiency — sounds like it's been quietly running in the background for a long time, maybe even before this diagnosis. What's so important to name is that this voice isn't just protecting you from disappointment; it's also keeping you at a distance from the very thing you're afraid of losing — real connection. I'm curious where that belief first took root for you — does it feel like something you learned, maybe from early experiences of what happened when you *did* need someone?

client: Yeah, I think... it probably does go back pretty far. I remember being a kid and my parents were always so stressed, always dealing with their own stuff, and I learned pretty quickly that bringing my problems to them just made things worse — like I was adding to the pile. So I guess I just started handling things on my own, telling myself that was just being mature or independent, not that I was scared of being too much for people.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — a young version of you made a very smart adaptation to a difficult situation, learning to shrink your needs to protect the people you loved and to protect yourself from disappointment. But what was a survival strategy for a child has quietly become a rule you're still living by, even now when the people around you may be very different from those stressed, overwhelmed parents. I'm wondering — if you could separate that old learned rule from what's actually true about you and the people in your life today, what might you allow yourself to believe about whether you deserve to be supported?

client: That's... a lot to sit with, honestly. Part of me wants to believe that I deserve support, that it's okay to ask for it, but there's this immediate pushback in my chest, like some voice saying "yeah, but what if you're still too much, even now?" I think I'm scared that if I test that old rule and find out it's still true, that people really don't want to hear what I need, that would hurt so much more than just staying quiet.
therapist: There's something really tender in what you're describing — that the very act of hoping things could be different feels dangerous, because hope means risk, and risk means the possibility of a pain that feels unbearable. What strikes me is that staying quiet has felt like protection, but it's also meant carrying all of this alone, including this diagnosis, which is an enormous weight for one person. I want to gently ask — has there been even one small moment, maybe recently or in the past, where you let someone in just a little and it didn't go the way that old voice predicted?

client: I've been sitting with that question and... there was this one time, maybe six months ago, when I told my coworker Sarah that I was having a really hard week. I didn't say anything about the diagnosis, just that things felt heavy, and she actually stayed late to eat lunch with me that day. But I keep telling myself that was small, that it doesn't really count, because if she knew the whole truth she'd probably pull away like everyone else does.
therapist: What Sarah did that day actually matters a great deal — she didn't pull away from your pain, she moved *toward* you, and that's real evidence that deserves to be taken seriously rather than explained away. I notice how quickly your mind discounted it with "that was small, it doesn't count" — that's the old protective voice working hard to keep the rule intact, because if Sarah's response *does* count, then the belief that you're too much for people starts to crack open. What do you think it would mean for that old story if you allowed yourself to let that moment count as real evidence?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe it... but it's scary, honestly. Like, if I let that moment count, and then Sarah eventually does pull away, it's going to hurt so much more than if I'd just kept my guard up. I think that's why my mind jumps so fast to "it was nothing" — it feels safer to stay small and not hope too much.
therapist: What you're describing is so deeply human — keeping hope small feels like the only way to keep the hurt manageable, and there's a real logic to that protection. But I want to reflect something back gently: you've already been carrying significant pain by staying small and guarded, so the question isn't really "pain or no pain" — it's whether the pain of staying closed off is more bearable than the risk of being truly seen. I'm wondering, when you imagine a version of yourself who let that moment with Sarah count, who allowed a little more hope — does that feel frightening, or is there also something in you that feels quietly drawn to it?

client: Honestly, when I picture that version of myself... there's something that does pull at me a little, like a small flicker of something I don't quite have a name for. But almost immediately I feel this wave of anxiety, like I'm already bracing for the disappointment that would come if I let myself believe Sarah actually wants to be close to me. It's like the hopeful part of me and the scared part of me are fighting, and the scared part has just had so much more practice winning.
therapist: That flicker you're describing — even without a name for it yet — is really worth paying attention to, because it's telling you something true about what you actually want, underneath all the years of practice the scared part has had. It makes so much sense that the anxious part moves faster and feels louder; it's had a lifetime of reinforcement, while that hopeful part is newer and more fragile, like a muscle that hasn't been used much yet. I'm curious — what do you think that small flickering part of you is reaching toward, if you let yourself listen to it just for a moment without the scared part interrupting?

client: I sit with that question for a second, and it's uncomfortable because I don't usually let myself go there. I think... it's reaching toward feeling like I actually belong somewhere, like there's a place or a group of people where I don't have to perform or explain myself. But even saying that out loud feels almost embarrassing, like I'm admitting to wanting something I'm not sure I'm allowed to have.
therapist: What you just named — belonging, being known without having to perform or explain — that's not an embarrassing want, that's one of the most fundamental human needs there is, and the fact that it feels almost forbidden to you says so much about how long you've had to earn your place in spaces rather than simply *be* in them. I want to gently push back on that word "allowed" — because it suggests belonging is something you have to qualify for, when really it's something you deserve simply by being a person who shows up honestly, exactly the way you're doing right now. What would it feel like to treat that longing for belonging not as something shameful to hide, but as something worth actually moving toward?
